transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-12 14:00 PST | Duration: 48 minutes | Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recording/ff-20251212-9b7e
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (Redwood), Asha Kapoor (Meridian Head of ML), Tom Bell (Infra Lead), Jian Li (Product), Sonia Verma (CTO)

Agenda: 1) Understand Meridian's workload and budget constraints 2) Agree on POC success criteria 3) Scope benchmarks and timelines 4) Define next steps

00:00:05 Lina: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intros, i know some folks we haven't met. i'm lina, i'm the AE working with meridian. marco and priya are from my solutions team.
00:00:18 Asha: hi, i'm asha, run the ml team. quick note, we got an NDA in place, so we can share traces.
00:00:25 Marco: great, thanks. to kick off — high level, meridian's ask is around cost modeling for a pilot plus a benchmark to validate both latency and cost at expected scale, correct?
00:00:38 Sonia: yup. we run an r-a-g flow inside our product search assistant. average prompt is about 120 tokens, answer ~80 tokens, but there's a long tail during debugging sessions.
00:00:51 Tom: infra wise we run on GCP, customers are east-us heavy — typical 70% traffic. we currently proxy requests through our gateway and hit OpenAI for final generations.
00:01:04 Lina: perfect. a couple of clarifying q's before we jump into unit econ: what's your target monthly budget for production if the pilot looks good?
00:01:12 Sonia: ballpark we'd like to keep inference spend under $12k/month initially. if the economics make sense we can scale up.
00:01:20 Asha: and our internal target p95 latency for the assistant is 350ms or better for interactive queries.
00:01:28 Marco: good — two concrete targets: cost target ~<$12k / month for initial run and p95 <350ms. got it.
00:01:34 Jian: scope — pilot should be 4 weeks of running real traffic mirrored from prod, plus one week of dedicated benchmarking. timeline wise we want to start benchmarks before year-end, ideally week of 12/22.
00:01:48 Lina: ok. let me walk through how we typically approach the cost model and where the knobs are. there are three main levers: 1) model choice and quantization, 2) batching and request concurrency, 3) prefix/K V cache hit rate — we call it prefix cache in the console.
00:02:03 Priya: (slight overlap) also whether you go Redwood Hosted or Dedicated capacity affects per-token unit cost — dedicated reserved pools reduce unit cost but add commit.
00:02:12 Asha: would you give us a baseline per-token estimate for a 13B-ish open model vs a 70B quantized? just to anchor expectations.
00:02:22 Marco: sure. for rough estimates at pilot scale: a 13B open model on hosted, with int8 quantization, tends to land around $0.00012-$0.00025 per input token and $0.00018-$0.00035 per output token depending on batching. for a 70B quantized variant it's higher: roughly $0.00035-$0.0009 per token if you're not aggressively batching or caching. those are ballparks — we'll run the benchmark to narrow them.
00:03:02 Tom: those ranges are wider than i expected. can you explain batching impact numerically?
00:03:08 Marco: absolutely. batching is one of the largest levers. if you can batch 8 requests together you amortize the per-step kernel cost. for example, a 13B model with avg seq len 200 (prompt+response) at batch size 1 might cost X, at batch 8 it can drop unit cost by 45-60% depending on GPU and kernel. i'll put actual sample spreadsheets in the pricing doc.
00:03:38 Asha: what about cache? our RAG flow should have high reuse on top-k doc prompts — what hit rate should we model?
00:03:45 Priya: we've seen enterprise customers get 30-60% effective prefix cache hit depending on how deterministic the prompt prefix is. for search assistants that reuse the same system prompt and some parts of user context, 40% is a reasonable planning assumption. higher if you control the client to reuse keys.
00:04:02 Sonia: so with 40% cache hit how does that change cost?
00:04:07 Marco: if 40% of the token generation is served from KV cache the effective tokens hitting the model are reduced — you can see a linear reduction in token compute. so if your average total tokens are 200 and 40% are cache hits, model tokens drop to ~120 effective tokens which reduces cost proportionally.
00:04:28 Jian: ok. for success criteria let's put them on record: 1) p95 latency <350ms on interactive flows, 2) effective cost < $0.0005 per total token averaged across pilot workload, 3) quality parity within existing tolerances (we'll use our eval prompts). sound fair?
00:04:46 Lina: yes that's a good starting S C R. we should explicitly define 'quality parity' as: match or exceed current OpenAI baseline on our 50 eval prompts with no more than 8% regression in accuracy/fluency metrics. we'll add that to the eval plan.
00:04:59 Asha: agreed. what about throughput — we have a peak of about 220 qps during business hours and about 9k daily active requests.
00:05:10 Marco: helpful. for sizing, that peak suggests we need concurrency headroom and proper autoscaling. for the pilot we'll recommend a small cluster sized for sustained 250 qps with 2x burst capability. we'll dimension GPUs based on model choice — i'll run numbers in the spreadsheet.
00:05:30 Tom: security question — we need VPC peering and customer-managed keys. can redwood support a private deployment or VPC peered dedicated setup?
00:05:40 Priya: yes — Redwood Private supports VPC peering and bring-your-own-KMS. for the pilot we usually run a dedicated capacity with VPC peering to avoid data egress complexity. there's a short onboarding for network configs.
00:05:52 Sonia: and audit logs / retention?
00:05:56 Lina: Console includes per-request logs and audit trails; retention is configurable as an add-on. we'll share the SOC/ISO pack as part of the security docs.
00:06:06 Asha: great. now benchmarks — what should we run during that week?
00:06:10 Marco: two phases. Phase A: synthetic replay using your anonymized traces at production scale to validate throughput and latency. Phase B: controlled microbenchmarks — variety of seq lens and batch sizes to map latency/cost curves. we'll run both 95th & 99th latency and get token-level cost breakdowns from the console.
00:06:31 Jian: can you surface per-route token/cost breakdown? we want to isolate heavy outliers — e.g., debug endpoints that generate long outputs.
00:06:39 Lina: yes, Console gives per-route and per-token breakdown. we can also provide a custom dashboard for the pilot to show cost per conversation and cache hit delta.
00:06:48 Asha: about timeline — you said benchmarks week of 12/22. if we need VPC peering, how long to onboard?
00:06:54 Priya: typical network onboarding for peering is 3-5 business days if firewall rules are straightforward. certificate exchange + KMS mapping another 2 days. so starting benchmarks 12/22 is tight but doable if we start network setup this week.
00:07:09 Tom: we'll prioritize it.
00:07:12 Marco: on instrumentation — we'll need: 1) anonymized request traces (JSON lines with timestamps and token counts), 2) expected traffic replay window (eg 1 hour of peak), 3) a small eval prompt set for quality checks.
00:07:27 Asha: we'll prepare that — can you accept S3 or GCP bucket shares?
00:07:31 Lina: both are fine. we'll share secure upload instructions.
00:07:35 Sonia: a question on economics: if we do dedicated reserved capacity how does that change the monthly math vs hosted? give us an example for clarity.
00:07:44 Marco: high level: Hosted = pay-as-you-go with higher per-token, low commit. Dedicated = monthly commit with lower per-token. Example: for a 13B quantized on hosted you might see ~$0.00025 per token; on dedicated with a 3-month commit and decent utilization that can drop to ~$0.00012 per token. exact depends on commit level and batchiness. we'll model 3 scenarios in the sheet: hosted, small dedicated (medium commit), and larger reserved.
00:08:12 Tom: what utilization numbers do you assume to get that discount?
00:08:16 Marco: typically 40-70% utilization — the higher you maintain the better the effective unit cost. we'll show sensitivity for 35%, 55%, 75% utilization.
00:08:26 Asha: ok that helps. for quality regression alerts — can we tie to our eval sets so if quality drops during rollout we get notified?
00:08:33 Priya: yes, Redwood Optimize supports eval-based monitors with regression thresholds. we can wire alerts to your slack or pager.
00:08:40 Jian: the customer-side effort — what's our expected involvement during the pilot?
00:08:44 Lina: from your side: share traces, give an engineering point of contact for peering, and validate outputs on the eval set weekly. Redwood will run the benchmarks, tune batching/quant configs, and provide remediation recommendations.
00:09:00 Sonia: any risk areas we should be aware of?
00:09:04 Marco: a few: 1) low batchability in interactive flows reduces unit-econ wins, 2) long-tail sequences increase cost unpredictably, 3) if your traffic isn't cache-friendly the KV cache helps less. we mitigate by tuning prompt engineering, increasing client-side request coalescing where possible, and selecting quantization profiles that optimize latency/cost tradeoffs.
00:09:27 Asha: sample question — can you run a quick thought experiment: with our numbers (9k daily requests, avg 200 tokens total, 40% cache, target <$12k/month), is that achievable?
00:09:40 Marco: quick calc: 9k requests * 200 tokens = 1.8M tokens/day = ~54M tokens/month. with 40% cache effective tokens = 32.4M. to hit $12k/month you need effective token cost ~ $0.00037 per token. that's in-range for a 13B quantized on dedicated with decent batching. so yes, it's plausible but depends on batching and model choice. we'll model exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
00:10:10 Tom: good to see the math.
00:10:12 Lina: ok let's capture the POC success criteria formally — I'll add them to the follow-up: 1) p95 <350ms on mirrored traffic during pilot, 2) blended cost <= $0.0005 per total token (or <$12k/mo for your projected traffic), 3) quality regression <8% on eval set, 4) secure VPC peering and KMS working in pilot environment.
00:10:31 Asha: agreed. next, any recommended microbench shapes you want us to include?
00:10:36 Marco: include short chat-like prompts (50 tokens), medium informative queries (200 tokens), and long debug flows (>=800 tokens). for each shape run batch sizes 1,4,8 and both cold cache and warmed cache runs. also run some concurrent arrival patterns to simulate peak.
00:10:55 Priya: we'll also test kv cache hit rates by replaying the same prefix for a subset of traffic to observe effective hit rates in practice.
00:11:03 Sonia: who will own the benchmark execution?
00:11:06 Marco: Redwood will run the controlled microbenchmarks, and we'll coordinate with Tom to replay the anonymized traces from your buckets for the synthetic production replay.
00:11:15 Tom: fine. what about telemetry access? we need to pull logs into our splunk.
00:11:19 Lina: we can stream request logs to your SIEM or provide S3 exports. we'll include both options in the ops doc.
00:11:27 Asha: any special config for token counting? we've seen differences between providers on how tokens are counted (esp with tokenizer choice).
00:11:33 Marco: yes, tokenization differences matter — we'll run tokenization parity checks and normalize counts to a single tokenizer we both agree on for pricing. we typically use the same byte-pair tokenizer we use in the Console for the model family selected.
00:11:48 Jian: can the pricing spreadsheet show scenario sensitivity for cache hit rate and batch size? that's huge for stakeholders.
00:11:55 Lina: yes — we'll include a sensitivity table: x-axis batch size (1/2/4/8/16), y-axis cache hit (0/20/40/60/80%), and show monthly cost across three model choices.
00:12:06 Asha: perfect.
00:12:09 Marco: quick note — sometimes customers are surprised by latency vs cost tradeoffs: if you push for lowest latency unbatched you pay a lot. conversely heavy batching lowers unit cost but increases tail latency. in your SLA window 350ms p95 we can still batch some requests if we're smart about routing — low-latency route for interactive sessions and a cost-optimized route for background tasks.
00:12:33 Sonia: sounds like we need routing policies. is that supported?
00:12:36 Priya: yes — Smart routing lets you define policies per route: low-latency model variant, fallback to cheaper variants outside business hours, and region-based routing to keep traffic close to users.
00:12:47 Tom: any practical gotchas when we do VPC peering and dedicated? e.g., NAT or egress costs?
00:12:52 Lina: main things: setup firewall rules so the peering CIDR is allowed, and depending on region there might be egress fees for cross-cloud. we'll run a quick network checklist with you and surface potential egress costs.
00:13:05 Asha: ok, let's talk deliverables: when can we expect the pricing spreadsheet and the benchmark plan?
00:13:10 Lina: i'll send the pricing spreadsheet and perf template by EOD 12/15. marco will send a draft of the benchmark steps by 12/16. then we can schedule the window with Tom for 12/22.
00:13:22 Tom: works for me, pending network prep.
00:13:24 Jian: final Q — any internal Redwood contacts for escalation on infra or security?
00:13:29 Lina: yes — i'll cc rajiv (support ops) and emily (security lead) on the follow-up thread. we'll include security docs. 
00:13:36 Asha: thanks.
00:13:39 Marco: okay that's the meat of it — any other blockers?
00:13:42 Sonia: none from exec. appreciate the clarity.
00:13:46 Lina: great. quick recap then next steps: 1) Lina share pricing spreadsheet & sensitivity table by 12/15 2) Marco share benchmark steps by 12/16 3) Meridian to upload traces and confirm POC contact + network windows by 12/18 4) schedule benchmark run for week of 12/22.
00:14:05 Asha: confirmed.
00:14:08 Lina: perfect — we'll follow up in the email and post the artifacts in the shared drive. thanks everyone.
00:14:15 (meeting off-record chatter and wrap up)
